definition: The item that was accessed most recently. In an LRU cache's recency list the MRU end is where touched items move to, and the opposite end holds the least recently used item, which is evicted first.
example: After get(B), B sits at the MRU end of the list.

definition: A cache that, when full, evicts the key with the fewest recorded accesses, usually breaking ties by evicting the least recently used of those keys. An O(1) design keeps one recency-ordered bucket per access count plus the smallest count currently in use.
example: With counts A=5, B=2, D=1, E=1, an LFU cache evicts D or E (whichever was used longer ago) before touching A.

definition: Removing a cache entry under an eviction policy, often to satisfy a capacity or memory limit. LRU targets least-recently used entries, LFU low recorded frequencies and FIFO oldest insertion order; admission, expiry and eviction are separate policy decisions.
example: A 3-item LRU cache holding A, B, C (C least recent) evicts C when D is inserted.

definition: An eviction policy approximating least-recently-used order, for example by sampling keys and preferring an older sampled entry. It can reduce exact-recency bookkeeping and contention; actual speed and concurrency costs depend on implementation.
example: Redis samples 5 keys per eviction by default (maxmemory-samples 5) and evicts the least recently used of them, helped by a pool of good candidates.

definition: A high-performance in-memory caching library for Java. Instead of exact LRU or LFU it uses the W-TinyLFU policy, which estimates access frequency with a compact frequency sketch.
A stack that also returns its current minimum in O(1) time. Each entry stores its value together with the minimum of everything at or below it, so popping restores the previous minimum automatically.
example: Pushing 5, 3, 7 stores (5,5), (3,3), (7,3); get_min returns 3, and after two pops it returns 5.

definition: A design exercise: store several timestamped values per key and answer "what was the value of this key at time t?". Appending values in time order and binary-searching the timestamps gives O(log n) lookups for n stored versions of a key.
example: With versions at times 1, 4 and 9, asking for time 6 returns the value written at time 4.

definition: A counted-key design supporting increment, decrement and retrieval of some minimum-count or maximum-count key. A key-to-bucket map and a linked list of count buckets make each change local under expected constant-time hashing and word-sized counts; it generalises the frequency-bucket idea used in LFU.
A number from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain) measuring how likely an event is. When every outcome is equally likely, it is the number of outcomes in the event divided by the total number of outcomes.
example: Picking one slot of [1, 1, 2] uniformly gives the value 1 with probability 2/3.

definition: The long-run average of a random quantity: each possible value weighted by its probability and added up. "Expected O(log n)" means the cost averaged over the structure's own random choices grows like log n, though any single run can be higher.
example: A fair die has expected value (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6 = 3.5.

definition: A mechanism that lets only one thread (or, for a read-write lock, either one writer or many readers) use shared data at a time, so concurrent updates cannot interleave and corrupt it. Locks are simple but make other threads wait.
example: Wrapping each LRU get and put in one lock makes the cache safe, but all threads then queue for it.

definition: Coordinating threads that share data so that they see consistent values and do not overwrite each other's changes, using locks, atomic operations or memory-ordering rules.

A progress property of a concurrent algorithm: among active threads, some operation finishes after finitely many algorithm steps, even if other threads pause. It gives system-wide progress, rather than a bounded completion time for each particular thread; atomic compare-and-swap is often used.
example: One thread can repeatedly lose a compare-and-swap race while other threads complete operations.

definition: A marker left in place of a deleted entry instead of removing it immediately. Lookups skip it and the space is reclaimed later; it is a common alternative to restructuring on every delete.

The standard way to implement union-find: each group is a tree stored only as parent pointers, and the tree's root is the group's representative. A whole forest of such trees fits in one array, parent[x].
example: parent = [0, 0, 1, 3, 3] encodes the groups {0, 1, 2} (root 0) and {3, 4} (root 3).

definition: The one element of a union-find group that stands for the whole group: the root of its tree. find(x) returns it, so two elements are in the same group exactly when find gives the same representative for both.
example: With parent = [0, 0, 1, 3, 3], find(2) returns 0, the representative of the group {0, 1, 2}.

definition: In Union-Find, a non-negative integer used to choose which root becomes a child. Merging distinct equal-rank roots raises the surviving rank by one; unequal-rank merges attach the lower rank below the higher. Compression can lower height without changing rank, so rank is an upper bound rather than current height.
example: Merging two rank-1 roots gives a rank-2 root; hanging a rank-0 root under it leaves the rank at 2.

definition: A Union-Find balancing rule that attaches the smaller component’s root under the larger component’s root. Every increase in an element’s depth at least doubles its component size, so depth is bounded by the base-two logarithm of the element count.
example: Merging a 3-element group into a 10-element group makes the 10-element root the new root.

definition: A one-pass alternative to full path compression in union-find: while walking up during find, point every other node at its grandparent. It gives the same inverse-Ackermann amortised bound with a simpler loop.
example: On a chain 4 → 3 → 2 → 1 → 0, path halving makes 4 point at 2 and 2 point at 0.

definition: A rapidly growing function on pairs of non-negative integers, defined recursively. Under the Ackermann–Péter convention its diagonal values include 3, 7 and 61 at arguments one, two and three, then an enormous tower of twos at four. Its growth is not primitive recursive; a slow-growing inverse describes Union-Find bounds.
example: A(4, 4) equals 2 to the power (2 to the power (2 to the power 65536)) minus 3.

definition: A model for data-structure lower bounds in which memory-cell accesses are counted and other computation is free. A bound transfers to implementations that fit the model’s word size and allowed operations; it is not a claim about every possible physical computer.
example: Fredman and Saks (1989) proved matching inverse-Ackermann amortised lower bounds for suitable Union-Find operation sequences in the cell-probe model.

definition: An American computer scientist, co-winner of the 1986 Turing Award, who proved the inverse-Ackermann bound for union-find (1975) and devised many graph algorithms and data structures, including splay trees and persistent structures with Driscoll, Sarnak and Sleator.
A set with exactly one element. Union-find starts with every element in its own singleton set, so n elements begin as n groups.

The study of whether a path connects one side of a randomly filled grid to the other. Union-find answers it by joining open neighbouring cells and checking whether a virtual top node and a virtual bottom node share a root.
example: On a large square grid of randomly opened sites, the system percolates once about 59 % of sites are open.

definition: Using random sampling to estimate an answer, such as repeating a random experiment many times and averaging. A Monte Carlo algorithm is a randomised algorithm with a bounded running time whose answer may be wrong with a small probability.
example: Estimating the percolation threshold by filling many random grids and recording when each percolates is a Monte Carlo experiment.

definition: Finding records that refer to the same real-world person or thing, such as customer entries sharing a phone number or email, and merging them. Union-find groups records that are linked directly or through chains of shared attributes.

A classic union-find exercise: given accounts as a name plus email addresses, merge every pair of accounts that share an email, directly or through a chain of other accounts, and list each person's emails.

A family of statically typed functional programming languages, including Standard ML and OCaml, known for Hindley–Milner type inference, which works out types without annotations by unifying type variables.

Solving equations between symbolic expressions by finding values for their variables that make both sides equal. Type checkers use it to infer types, and a union-find structure tracks which type variables have been made equal.
example: Unifying list(α) with list(int) sets α = int.

definition: A union-find variant where each node stores a value relative to its parent, such as an offset, ratio or parity bit. find combines the values along the path, so the structure can answer relationships like "a is 6 times c" between any two connected elements.
example: Storing a/b = 2 and b/c = 3 on parent edges lets find work out a/c = 6.

definition: An algorithm that knows requests in advance and may process them in a convenient order. For a known deletion-only edge history, initialise Union-Find with the final graph and reverse the deletions into additions; mixed additions and deletions need additional machinery.

For a connected undirected graph formed from a tree plus one edge, removing any edge on its unique cycle leaves a tree. Processing edges in input order with Union-Find identifies the edge that first closes that cycle; this need not identify which edge was historically added.

An incremental-connectivity exercise: add land cells to a grid and report the number of connected land groups after each addition. A DSU solution creates a component for new land and merges it with each existing neighbouring land component; duplicate additions need an explicit check.

A deferred update stored at a lazy segment-tree node. The node’s own summary already includes the update, while its children may still need it. Before descending, push that update into the child summaries and compose their tags, then clear the parent tag.
example: A tag of +5 on node [0,3] becomes tags of +5 on [0,1] and [2,3] when pushed down.

definition: The largest total of any contiguous run of an array's elements. A segment tree can maintain it under point updates by storing four numbers per node: total, best prefix, best suffix and best subarray.
example: For [2, −1, 3, −5] the maximum subarray sum is 4, from 2 − 1 + 3.

definition: A one-pass O(n) algorithm for the maximum subarray sum of a fixed array: at each position keep the best sum of a subarray ending there, which is either the element alone or the element added to the previous best. It cannot handle updates without starting again.
example: On [2, −1, 3, −5] the best sums ending at each position are 2, 1, 4, −1, so the answer is 4.

definition: Replacing a set of large or sparse values with their ranks 0, 1, 2, … in sorted order, keeping their relative order. Fenwick and segment trees then need only as many slots as there are distinct values, not one per possible value.
example: The values [1000, 7, 1000000] compress to [1, 0, 2].

definition: A segment tree that creates nodes only when an operation first touches them, instead of allocating the whole tree up front. It can cover huge index ranges such as 0 to 10^9 using memory proportional to the number of operations times the tree height.
The branch of algorithms dealing with points, lines, polygons and other geometric objects, such as computing convex hulls, intersections or the area covered by a union of rectangles.
A query asking which stored intervals contain a given point. The computational-geometry segment tree answers it in O(log n + k) for n intervals and k results.
example: Intervals [1,5], [3,8], [9,12] queried at point 4 return the first two.

definition: A record type that groups several named fields into one value, such as a node holding sum, pre, suf and best together. Python code typically uses a tuple, small class or dataclass for the same purpose.

Work associated with function calls and stack frames rather than the data-structure operation itself. Replacing recursive calls with loops can reduce that overhead, but actual speed depends on implementation and workload and should be measured.

An operation where the order of the two inputs matters, so x ⊕ y can differ from y ⊕ x. Matrix multiplication and string concatenation are associative but non-commutative, so a segment tree must always combine the left child before the right.
example: "ab" + "cd" is "abcd" but "cd" + "ab" is "cdab".

definition: Short for binary indexed tree, another name for a Fenwick tree: one array in which entry i stores the sum of a block ending at i whose length is the lowest set bit of i, giving O(log n) prefix sums and point updates.

For a positive integer, the value of its rightmost set bit, equivalently the largest power of two dividing it. Python computes it as i & -i using its infinite-sign-bit model; fixed-width ports require suitable unsigned or non-overflowing arithmetic.
example: lowbit(12) = 4, because 12 is 1100 in binary; lowbit of any odd number is 1.

definition: A binary digit that is 1 rather than 0. A Fenwick prefix query takes one step per set bit of the index, so at most about log2(n) + 1 steps.
example: 13 is 1101 in binary and has three set bits.

definition: For a combine operation, a way to undo a value: combining x with its inverse gives the identity element. Subtraction undoes addition and XOR undoes itself, which is what lets a Fenwick tree get range sums from two prefix sums; min and max have no inverse.
example: Knowing the sum of a[1..7] and of a[1..2] gives the sum of a[3..7] by subtraction; knowing two minima does not.

definition: A set with an operation that is associative and commutative, has an identity element, and gives every element an inverse. Integers under addition and bit strings under XOR are abelian groups, which is exactly what a standard Fenwick tree needs.

Numbering array positions from 1 rather than 0. This Fenwick implementation reserves index 0: its lowbit is zero, so a point-update loop would never advance there. Zero-based input positions are shifted by one at the boundary.
example: Element a[0] of a 0-indexed Python list is stored at Fenwick position 1.

definition: The amount by which a value changes. A Fenwick tree's add(i, delta) increases element i by delta rather than setting it, so to set a[i] to x you add x − a[i].
example: Changing a[3] from 7 to 10 is add(3, 3).

definition: Short for "no operation": a call or instruction that deliberately does nothing. A Fenwick add at position n + 1 is a no-op because the loop condition fails immediately.
A table giving, for each symbol, how many times it or any earlier symbol occurred. Arithmetic coders need it updated after every symbol, the job Fenwick designed his tree for in 1994.
example: For counts a:3, b:5, c:2 the cumulative frequencies are 3, 8, 10.

definition: A Fenwick tree over a grid: t[i][j] with nested lowbit loops, giving rectangle prefix sums and point updates in O(log n · log m) on an n-by-m grid.

term: Count of smaller numbers after self
aliases: count of smaller numbers after self
definition: A classic exercise: for each array element, count how many later elements are smaller. Scanning from the right with a Fenwick tree of value counts answers it in O(n log n).
example: For [5, 2, 6, 1] the answer is [2, 1, 1, 0].

definition: An array whose entry i is the longest proper border length of the prefix ending at i: a prefix that is also a suffix but is not the whole prefix. KMP uses these lengths for fallbacks; related failure-table conventions can use different indexing or sentinel values.
example: For "ababa" the prefix function is [0, 0, 1, 2, 3].

definition: A string that is both a proper prefix and a suffix of another string. The prefix function stores the length of the longest border of each prefix of a pattern.
example: "aba" is a border of "ababa"; so is "a".

definition: A prefix (or suffix) of a string that is not the whole string. Requiring borders to be proper stops every string trivially matching itself.
example: The proper prefixes of "abc" are "", "a" and "ab".

definition: For a string s, the array whose entry i is the length of the longest substring starting at i that is also a prefix of s (z[0] is 0 by convention). It is computed in O(n) by reusing a window [l, r) already known to match the prefix.
example: For "aabxaab" the Z-array is [0, 1, 0, 0, 3, 1, 0].

definition: Two different inputs that produce the same hash value. They are unavoidable when there are more possible inputs than hash values, so Rabin–Karp treats a hash match only as a candidate and confirms it by comparing the strings.
example: With hashes mod 10, the windows "13" and "23" both hash to 3.

definition: A short hash value used to stand for a much longer piece of data, so two pieces can be compared quickly. Matching fingerprints suggest, but do not prove, that the data is equal.
For a suffix array, the array storing the length of the longest common prefix of each adjacent pair of sorted suffixes. It turns questions about repeated or distinct substrings into simple scans.
example: For "banana" the sorted suffixes give LCP values [0, 1, 3, 0, 0, 2]; the longest repeated substring has length 3 ("ana").

definition: An O(n) algorithm (Kasai et al., 2001) that builds the LCP array from a string and its suffix array, using the fact that the common-prefix length drops by at most one when moving from one suffix to the next shorter one.
An algorithm (Esko Ukkonen, 1995) that builds a suffix tree in linear time for a constant-size alphabet, adding one character at a time from left to right.

A linear-time suffix-array construction algorithm (Nong, Zhang and Chan, 2009) based on induced sorting: it sorts a few special suffixes recursively, then derives the order of all the others from them.

A linear-time suffix-array construction algorithm (Kärkkäinen and Sanders, 2003), also called the skew algorithm: it recursively sorts the suffixes at two-thirds of the positions and merges in the rest.

A way to build a suffix array by sorting suffixes by their first 1, 2, 4, 8, … characters, where each round reuses the previous round's ranks as pairs. It needs about log2(n) rounds, giving O(n log n) with radix sort.
The longest string occurring at least twice in a text; occurrences may overlap. Its length is the largest value in the LCP array.
example: In "banana" it is "ana", which occurs at positions 1 and 3.

definition: How many different strings occur as substrings of a text. It equals n(n + 1)/2 minus the sum of the LCP array, because each suffix's shared prefix with its sorted neighbour was already counted.
example: "banana" has 21 − 6 = 15 distinct non-empty substrings.

definition: A compressed full-text index (Ferragina and Manzini, 2000) built on the Burrows–Wheeler transform. It counts and locates pattern occurrences while using space close to the compressed size of the text, which is why genome aligners use it.

A reversible rearrangement of a string's characters, read off the last column of its sorted rotations. It groups similar characters together, which helps compression (bzip2) and underpins the FM-index.
example: The BWT of "banana$" is "annb$aa".

definition: A widely used tool that aligns short DNA sequencing reads to a reference genome, using an FM-index built on the Burrows–Wheeler transform.
A fast, memory-efficient aligner for short DNA sequencing reads that, like BWA, searches an FM-index of the reference genome.

An organism’s genetic material, often represented as a DNA-sequence string. A, C, G and T are the four standard DNA bases; real reference files may also include ambiguity symbols and gaps. Many human reference assemblies contain roughly three billion bases, with the exact size depending on the assembly.

Splitting bytes at boundaries selected from local content, often by a rolling fingerprint test. Insertions can let later boundaries resynchronise so unchanged chunks remain reusable; minimum/maximum chunk limits and the content can affect how far boundary changes propagate.
An open-source backup program that splits files with content-defined chunking (using a rolling Rabin fingerprint) and stores each distinct chunk once.

A file-synchronisation tool that sends only the parts of a file that changed. It checks every offset of the new file against fixed-size blocks of the old (basis) file using a cheap rolling checksum, confirming candidates with a stronger hash.

Pattern-search algorithms that use mismatch information to skip candidate positions; Boyer–Moore commonly compares backwards. Horspool simplifies the shift rule. Their realised speed depends on the pattern, text and implementation, rather than a universal “fast on ordinary text” guarantee.
A character placed between two strings when they are concatenated, chosen so it appears in neither, such as "#" in p + "#" + t. It stops a match or common prefix from running across the join.
The smallest shift p such that the string matches itself shifted by p: s[i] = s[i + p] wherever both exist. It can be read from the prefix function or the Z-function.
example: "abcabcab" has period 3.

definition: If more items are put into boxes than there are boxes, at least one box holds two items. It proves that any hash with fewer values than possible inputs must have collisions.
example: 2^80 possible 10-byte windows hashed into about 10^9 values must collide.

definition: An algorithm analysed using random choices, such as random priorities or a random fingerprint family. Depending on the algorithm and model, its cost or correctness is probabilistic. Fixed public hashes have deterministic collisions and need a stated random-input or random-hash model for probability claims.
The remainder left after dividing by a modulus M, one of 0, 1, …, M − 1. Numbers that leave the same residue are congruent mod M.
example: Both 4 and −7 are congruent mod 11, but only 4 is the standard residue.

definition: A structure that makes random choices, such as skip-list promotions or treap priorities. For fixed inputs independent of those choices, suitable models yield expected logarithmic operations and high-probability balance; an adaptive adversary or a fixed level cap changes the assumptions.
A guarantee that a bound fails only with a probability that shrinks quickly as n grows, typically at most 1/n^c for some constant c. It is stronger than a bound on the average alone.
An informal name for a skip list's upper levels: sparser linked lists that let a search jump over many nodes of the level below, like an express train skipping stations.
In a skip list, the chance p that a node on one level is also placed on the next level up. With p = 1/2 a node sits on 2 levels on average; with p = 1/4, on about 1.33.

A link from one skip-list node to the next node on the same level. A node occupying several levels has one forward pointer per level; keys, values, backward pointers, spans and allocation overhead can also contribute to memory.

For a Redis skip-list link with a forward target, its span is the target’s bottom-level rank minus the current node’s rank, including the destination. A tail link with no target counts remaining bottom-level nodes. Summing spans along a search gives rank; Redis ZRANK exposes zero-based member positions.

A Redis data type holding unique members each with a numeric score, kept ordered by score. Commands include ZADD (add or update), ZRANGE (read a range by position) and ZRANK (a member's position). Large sets use a hash table plus a skip list; small ones use a compact listpack.
example: A game leaderboard: ZADD scores 1500 "alice", then ZRANK scores "alice" gives her position.

definition: The in-memory, sorted write buffer of an LSM-tree storage engine such as LevelDB or RocksDB. New writes go into it, and when it fills it is written to disk as a sorted file.

A sorted concurrent map in java.util.concurrent, built with a skip-list implementation. Its Java SE 21 API documents expected average logarithmic get, put and remove operations and safe concurrent access; the public API does not promise lock-free progress.
A random number given to each treap node when it is created. The tree is kept heap-ordered on priorities, which makes its shape the same as a BST built by inserting keys in random order.

The two core treap operations. split(t, key) cuts a treap into one with keys below key and one with the rest; merge(a, b) joins two treaps when every key in a is smaller than every key in b. Insert, delete and range operations are built from them.

A treap representing a sequence by subtree sizes rather than stored position keys. With the required augmentations and independent random priorities, navigation, split and merge have expected logarithmic tree work. Inserting fresh text or items and reclaiming removed nodes add their own costs.
A binary tree built from a sequence that is heap-ordered on the values and gives back the original order in an in-order traversal. A treap is a Cartesian tree of (key, priority) pairs.
Storing extra information at each tree node, such as subtree size or sum, and keeping it correct during updates. It lets a balanced tree answer extra queries like "k-th smallest" in O(log n).
A family of algorithms that keep a uniform random sample of k items from a stream of unknown length in one pass, using only O(k) memory.
example: With a 10-slot reservoir over 1,000 log lines, every line ends up in the sample with probability 1 %.

definition: The basic reservoir-sampling procedure described as Algorithm R in Vitter’s 1985 paper, which credits Alan Waterman: keep the first k items, then draw uniformly among all positions seen and replace a reservoir slot only when that draw names one.

Li’s 1994 reservoir-sampling algorithm, which skips between selected replacements. Expected sampling work is on the order of sample size multiplied by one plus the logarithm of the population-to-sample ratio, ignoring input scanning. Constants and implementation determine actual random-draw counts.

Sampling where items have weights. The Efraimidis–Spirakis method gives each item the key u^(1/w), with u uniform between 0 and 1 and w its weight, and keeps the k largest keys; the result is weighted sampling without replacement.
Drawing items so that each can be chosen at most once, like dealing cards from a deck. Sampling with replacement puts each item back, so it can be drawn again.

The distribution of how many items of one kind appear in a sample drawn without replacement from a population with a known mix. It decides how many of a merged reservoir's k slots each shard should contribute.
example: Drawing 5 cards from a deck, the number of hearts follows a hypergeometric distribution.

definition: The chance that a particular item ends up in a random sample. In reservoir sampling it is k/n for every item, but equal inclusion probabilities alone do not prove every subset is equally likely.

A descending swap algorithm that chooses only an earlier index, excluding the current one. It generates every single-cycle permutation uniformly under independent uniform draws, so it is not uniform over all permutations of two or more distinct items.
A rearrangement in which following "where does this item go?" from any item visits every item before returning. There are (n − 1)! of them among the n! permutations of n items.
example: For 3 items, (1 2 3) → (2 3 1) is single-cycle; the identity is not.

definition: A comparison function that returns a random answer, such as () => Math.random() - 0.5 in JavaScript. Sorting with it gives biased, implementation-dependent orders because sorts assume comparisons are consistent.

Python random-number functions. randint(a, b) returns a whole number from a to b inclusive; randrange(b) returns one from 0 up to b − 1, excluding b. Mixing them up is a classic off-by-one bug in shuffles.
example: randint(0, 2) can return 2; randrange(2) never does.

definition: An algorithm that produces a sequence of numbers that look random but are fully determined by a starting seed. With a 32-bit seed it can produce at most about 4.3 billion different sequences.

Python’s SystemRandom uses the operating system’s cryptographically secure random source rather than the deterministic random-module generator. It is intended for unpredictable choices and relies on the security of that operating-system source.

A measure of uncertainty, in bits. For uniformly distributed outcomes, it is the base-two logarithm of the number of outcomes; a non-uniform distribution has lower entropy. A uniform permutation of 52 distinct cards has about 225.6 bits of entropy.
The distribution of how many coin flips it takes to get the first tails (or heads). Skip-list levels follow it: each extra level needs one more heads, so levels thin out by a factor p each time.
example: With p = 1/2, a node reaches level 3 or higher with probability 1/4.

definition: An American computer scientist who invented the skip list (published 1990), presenting it as a simpler probabilistic alternative to balanced trees.

An operation that gives the same result however many times it is applied. In algebra this means combining a value with itself gives it back: min(x, x) = x, so min, max, gcd, bitwise AND and OR are idempotent but addition is not; a sparse table's O(1) query needs it because its two blocks can overlap. In distributed systems it means repeating a request has the same effect as doing it once.
example: min(7, 7) = 7, but 7 + 7 = 14, so overlapping blocks would double-count a sum.

definition: A sparse-table variant that stores, for each level, prefix and suffix aggregates around block midpoints, so any range is answered by combining two non-overlapping pieces. It gives O(1) queries for associative operations that are not idempotent, such as sums or products.

Splitting an array into blocks and combining whole-block summaries with work at query edges. Generic square-root decomposition has square-root query costs. Linear-build, constant-time static RMQ needs a specialised micro/macro construction, not arbitrary block sizes.

A Python integer method returning how many bits are needed to write the number in binary, ignoring sign and leading zeros. For a positive x, x.bit_length() − 1 is the base-2 logarithm of x rounded down. Zero has bit_length zero.
example: (5).bit_length() is 3, because 5 is 101 in binary.

definition: A GCC built-in counting leading zero bits in an unsigned int. Its width depends on the implementation and zero input has undefined results for this built-in. For a positive 32-bit unsigned int, subtracting the count from 31 gives its base-two logarithm rounded down; hardware lowering depends on the target.
example: __builtin_clz(5) is 29, so 31 − 29 = 2.

definition: An ordinary data structure in which an update destroys the previous version, so only the current state can be read. It is the opposite of a persistent structure.
The property of a data structure that keeps its old versions usable after updates, usually by sharing unchanged parts between versions. It is unrelated to saving data to disk.
example: After inserting 45 by path copying, both the old root and the new root are valid trees.

definition: A persistent structure where every old version can be read but only the newest version can be updated, so the versions form a line.
A persistent structure where any version, old or new, can be both read and updated, so the versions form a tree rather than a line.

Making a tree persistent by copying only the nodes on the root-to-leaf path an update changes and pointing the copies at the old, unchanged subtrees. In a balanced tree that is O(log n) new nodes per update.
example: Inserting 45 into a tree with keys 20, 30, 40, 50, 70 copies 50, 30 and 40 and adds 45: four new nodes.

definition: A persistence technique in which each field keeps a list of (version, value) pairs instead of being overwritten. Reading an old version binary-searches that list.

A segment tree made persistent by path copying, keeping one root per version. With one version per array prefix over value ranks, subtracting two versions' counts answers "k-th smallest value in a[l..r]" in O(log n).

A sharing technique that postpones copying until a write needs an independent version. Writes copy the affected shared data while readers retain the original; exclusively owned data may sometimes be updated directly. LMDB and Btrfs use copy-on-write trees to maintain snapshots.

Lightning Memory-Mapped Database: an embedded key–value store built on a copy-on-write B+ tree in a memory-mapped file. Readers see a consistent snapshot without taking locks while a single writer prepares the next version.
A Linux file system built on copy-on-write B-trees, which lets it take cheap snapshots that share unchanged data with the live file system.
The PostgreSQL command that reclaims space taken by row versions no longer visible to any transaction. MVCC leaves old row versions in the table, and VACUUM (or autovacuum) cleans them up.

Git's object for a file's contents, named by the hash of those contents. Tree objects list blobs and sub-trees, and a commit points to one root tree, so unchanged files and folders are shared between commits.

A Lisp-family functional language on the JVM with persistent immutable collections. Its vectors use wide branching trees and a tail buffer; hash maps use hash-array mapped tries, collision nodes and specialised small-map forms. Updates share unchanged structure rather than universally copying one identical 32-way layout.
A functional programming language built for highly available telecom systems, in which data is immutable, so updates create new versions that share structure with the old.

A tree representing long text through smaller leaf chunks. The binary example stores each internal node’s left-subtree character length as its weight. Balanced, bounded-chunk implementations give logarithmic navigation, while insertion also processes the new characters and deletion may reclaim nodes.
example: Character 10 of "Hello_my_name_is_Simon" is found by comparing 10 with node weights on the way down.

definition: In a rope, the number stored at an internal node: the total length of the text in its left subtree. To find character i, go left if i is smaller than the weight, otherwise subtract the weight and go right.

A text-editor buffer that never edits the original file: it keeps the original text, an append-only buffer of added text, and a list of pieces saying which parts of each to show in order. VS Code stores its pieces in a red–black tree, the "piece tree".
Storage that is only ever added to at the end, never changed in place. A piece table puts all inserted text into one, so earlier pieces stay valid.

An experimental text-editor project started by Raph Levien, whose core used a persistent rope built from B-tree text chunks. The repository says the project is no longer maintained; this is a historical implementation example.
A code editor written in Rust that stores text in a rope-like B-tree of chunks (its "SumTree").
Microsoft’s open-source code editor. Its 2018 engineering account describes replacing the text buffer with a piece table backed by a red–black tree, avoiding whole-document copies during edits.
The Standard Template Library, the C++ container and algorithm library; SGI (Silicon Graphics) distributed an influential version of it that included a rope class not adopted by the C++ standard.
A compilation unit in Rust, either a binary or a library. A Cargo package contains one or more crates and a manifest. Ropey is a library crate that can be added as a package dependency.
A Rust crate implementing a UTF-8 text rope, designed for editors handling large files with frequent edits.

How effectively memory accesses reuse nearby or recently accessed data in CPU caches. Contiguous arrays often have better locality than scattered pointer nodes. Rope chunk size is an implementation and workload choice that balances this locality against editing costs.

Boehm, Atkinson and Plass described practical rope string representations in their 1995 paper “Ropes: an Alternative to Strings”. The paper discusses earlier Cedar ropes as well as their C implementation, so 1995 is not the date ropes first existed.

Authors of "Making Data Structures Persistent" (1989), which showed how to make linked structures with bounded in-degree persistent at O(1) amortised extra space per field change, using node copying and fat nodes.
